extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Alice/Mayo two-step §101 eligibility analysis, including Step 2A Prong Two (particular treatment/prophylaxis integration) and Step 2B (search for an inventive concept). Applicable to claim drafting and examination of medical, computer-implemented, and other claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Treatment and Prophylaxis (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; one way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an application/use meaningfully limits the claim by going beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment, transforming the claim into patent-eligible subject matter at Step 2A. See Vanda (distinguishing Mayo where administering step was ancillary vs Vanda where administration used the law of nature to more safely treat patients). Examples of treatment/prophylaxis include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, immunization, etc. (See Classen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative Recitation Requirement for Treatment/Prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a 'treatment' or 'prophylaxis' limitation, the claim limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of affirmative limitations: 'administering amazonic acid to a patient', 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient'. Non-qualifying language includes mere intended use, field-of-use, or prescriptions that do not require actual use (e.g., 'prescribing a topical steroid to a patient' is not positive because it does not require that the steroid actually be used; 'pharmaceutical composition' or 'feed dispenser operable to dispense' are not affirmative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity (Specificity) of the Treatment or Prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular', i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific administration step tied to the identified exception (e.g., 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype') integrates the abstract idea into a practical application. A generic instruction (e.g., 'administering a suitable medication to a patient') is not particular and fails to integrate the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: More-Than-Nominal Relationship to the Judicial Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the recited judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed treatment meaningfully addresses the recited law/correlation (e.g., treating blood glucose >250 mg/dl with insulin meaningfully relates to the correlation and integrates the law of nature; treating with aspirin, not known to treat ketoacidosis, has at best a nominal connection and does not integrate the law of nature). See guidance to consider insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations (MPEP § 2106.05(g),(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not Mere Extra-Solution Activity or Field-Of-Use
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be merely extra-solution activity or a field-of-use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a physical step is performed only to gather data needed for an abstract mental step (i.e., a necessary precursor for all uses of the exception), it may be extra-solution activity and not integrate the exception. Contrast: vaccinating a first group to gather data (extra-solution) vs vaccinating a second group according to the derived lowest-risk schedule (applies the exception and integrates it). See MPEP §2106.04(d)(2) examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an Inventive Concept (Step 2B) — Overarching Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'inventive concept' is an element or combination of elements recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception that is sufficient to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself; it cannot be furnished by the judicial exception alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate additional elements to determine whether they amount to an inventive concept by considering them both individually and in combination. The analysis is consistent with the rule that claims must be considered as a whole; combinations of conventional elements can, in some cases, amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Elements Individually And In Combination
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating additional elements for an inventive concept, consider each additional element on its own and also consider the elements as an ordered combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an element does not amount to significantly more by itself, it can when combined with other elements (e.g., BASCOM: location of filtering tool remote from end-users with customizable features produced an inventive concept when considered in combination). Courts identify additional elements, assess conventionality, and then assess whether the claimed combination is non-conventional and non-generic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive-Concept Inquiry Is Distinct From Novelty/Obviousness (35 U.S.C. §§102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept under §101 is not a substitute for inquiries under §§102, 103, or 112; novelty/non-obviousness are of no relevance in determining whether subject matter falls within §101 categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of novelty or obviousness does not indicate whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, or conventional for §101 purposes. Do not conflate inventive-concept analysis with prior-art patentability inquiries (see Mayo, Diamond, Intellectual Ventures, Synopsys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement To The Functioning Of A Computer Can Be 'Significantly More'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve the functioning of a computer (e.g., modification of conventional internet hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a dual-source hybrid webpage) can qualify as an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See DDR Holdings example; improvements to computer operation or behavior may establish significantly more when the claim is not merely applying an abstract idea on a generic computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement To Another Technology Or Technical Field Can Be 'Significantly More'
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that improve the functioning of any other technology or technical field (e.g., modifications to rubber-molding processes with a thermocouple to improve curing) can qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Diamond v. Diehr example; an improvement to a technological process that produces a practical result can satisfy Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying The Judicial Exception With Or By Use Of A Particular Machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine arranged in a specific way can constitute an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: arranging a Fourdrinier machine in a particular way to optimize speed while maintaining quality (Eibel Process Co.). Mere recitation of a generic machine is insufficient; the specific machine/arrangement must meaningfully contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting A Transformation Or Reduction Of A Particular Article
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that effect a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming raw uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr). The claimed process must effect a concrete transformation, not merely apply an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding Specific Limitations Or Unconventional Steps That Confine The Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of computer components for filtering Internet content (BASCOM). The presence of unconventional arrangement or confinement to a useful application supports eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Meaningful Limitations Beyond Generally Linking Use To Technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment can constitute significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an immunization step that integrates data comparison into a specific immunizing process that lowers later disease risk (Classen). The limitation must be more than a general tie to a technological environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding 'Apply It' Or Mere Computer Implementation Is Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the words 'apply it' (or equivalent) with the judicial exception, or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, does not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: limitations indicating that a function (e.g., creating and maintaining electronic records) is performed by a computer are 'well-understood, routine, conventional' and insufficient (Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appending Well-Understood, Routine, Conventional Activities Is Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, will not make a claim significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic computer functions performed by a generic computer are inadequate. The inventive-concept inquiry looks for more than recognition that each claim element was known in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity Is Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering) to the judicial exception does not amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: obtaining information about transactions so it can be analyzed by an abstract mental process (CyberSource). Consider the 'insignificant extra-solution activity' doctrine in analysis (MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally Linking The Exception To A Technical Environment Or Field-Of-Use Is Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field-of-use does not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: limiting a mathematical formula to petrochemical fields or stating that hedging is used in commodities markets (Parker v. Flook; Bilski). High-level field-of-use limitations are inadequate (see MPEP § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/Tangibility Is Not A Determinative Factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B; a computer being physical does not by itself supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a tangible element does not guarantee eligibility (Alice). Conversely, non-physical or intangible additional elements do not necessarily doom eligibility (Enfish, McRO). Focus on what the claim adds conceptually and functionally, not mere physical presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: How Courts Conduct The Significantly-More Analysis (Alice and BASCOM Examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts identify additional elements, consider those elements individually (including conventionality), and then consider the elements as an ordered combination to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice: Court identified additional computer/hardware elements, found each to be generic and routine, then concluded the ordered combination added nothing (claims ineligible). BASCOM: district court identified elements as generic, but Federal Circuit held the combination (installation location + customizable features) could be non-conventional and thus supply an inventive concept. Consult the specification to determine whether elements are well-understood, routine, conventional.
